title: ClickHouse Administration & Distributed Operations: Level 2 Workshop (CH-201 to CH-204)
summary:
A Level 2 technical workshop from ChistaDATA on replication, Keeper, sharding and ingestion: how a ClickHouse cluster stays consistent, where it breaks, and the rehearsed procedures that bring it back. Checked against ClickHouse 26.3 and 26.8 LTS, with labs and fault drills run on a dedicated 2 x 2 cluster with its own three-node Keeper ensemble and a Kafka broker.

Four modules, about 14 hours, instructor-led and hands-on:

CH-201 Replication internals: the replicated log and queue, system.replicas as a health surface, stuck-entry triage, and four rehearsed recovery scenarios.

CH-202 Keeper: Raft mechanics, quorum arithmetic, snapshots and logs, coordination-data backup, mntr monitoring, and three fault drills.

CH-203 Distributed tables: fan-out and initial_query_id tracing, write paths, sharding keys against hot shards, GLOBAL IN and JOIN, and resharding.

CH-204 Ingestion engineering: Kafka consumer semantics, the Kafka engine to materialized view to MergeTree boundary, async inserts, deduplication windows, outage arithmetic and SLOs.

Written for CTOs, architects, SREs, DBAs and data engineers who run ClickHouse in production. Prerequisite: Level 1, ClickHouse Internals Foundations (CH-101 to CH-105): https://speakerdeck.com/shiviyer007/clickhouse-internals-foundations-level-1-workshop-ch-101-to-ch-105

Presented by Shiv Iyer, Founder and CEO, ChistaDATA Inc.
https://chistadata.com

The fault drills are designed for an isolated lab cluster. Do not run fault-injection steps against production or shared environments, and test on your own workload before applying anything to production.

title: ClickHouse Internals Foundations: Level 1 Workshop (CH-101 to CH-105)
summary:
A Level 1 technical workshop from ChistaDATA on how ClickHouse works underneath: how it executes a query, writes and merges parts, prunes data, compresses columns and serves dictionaries. Behaviour and defaults were checked against ClickHouse 26.3 and 26.8 LTS, and every claim on the slides is backed by a query you can run on your own cluster.

Five modules, about 15 hours, instructor-led and hands-on:

CH-101 Architecture and execution: query lifecycle, vectorised block processing, the MergeTree family and the settings hierarchy.

CH-102 Parts and on-disk layout: part anatomy, the insert path and backpressure, merge selection, mutations as rewrites, granules and part states.

CH-103 Keys, indexes and projections: partition pruning and lifecycle, sort-key engineering with EXPLAIN indexes = 1, skip indexes, projections, and default changes between versions.

CH-104 Compression codecs: LZ4 and ZSTD trade-offs, Delta, DoubleDelta, Gorilla, T64, codec chaining rules, and a measurement loop over system.columns.

CH-105 Dictionaries: source wiring, layout selection and memory profile, lifetime and refresh, dictGet against JOIN, and operating through system.dictionaries.

Written for CTOs, architects, analytics engineers, data scientists, DBAs and data engineers.

Presented by Shiv Iyer, Founder and CEO, ChistaDATA Inc.
https://chistadata.com

Defaults change between releases, so read them from your own server and test on your own workload before applying anything to production.

title: Python Decorators from Syntactic Sugar to Production-Grade Design Tool
summary:
Python decorators are among Python's most powerful and elegant features. Although their syntax is relatively simple, their capabilities extend far beyond adding an @ symbol before a function or class definition.

In this talk, delivered at Python Summit 2026, I explore how Python decorators work, how to build your own decorators, and how to use them effectively in production-grade software.

We begin with the fundamentals, examining Python's support for first-class functions and understanding what actually happens behind the scenes when a decorator is applied. From there, we move on to more advanced techniques, including function-based decorators, class-based decorators, nested decorators, and decorators that accept arguments.

The presentation includes practical code examples showing how decorators separate responsibilities, reduce code duplication, and improve software maintainability.

We also explore real-world applications of decorators, including:

Execution Time Measurement: Measuring function performance without modifying the original implementation.

Logging: Tracking function calls, arguments, and return values.

Caching: Improving performance by avoiding unnecessary repeated computations.

RESTful Web Services: Understanding how FastAPI uses decorators to define API endpoints.

Command-Line Applications: Exploring how Typer uses decorators to simplify CLI development.

An important part of the talk focuses on best practices for developing reliable, reusable, and maintainable decorators. We discuss preserving function metadata with functools.wraps, supporting arbitrary function arguments using *args and **kwargs, following the Single Responsibility Principle (SRP), proper exception handling, documentation, unit testing, and type hinting.

As AI increasingly generates software, understanding good software design becomes even more important. AI can produce code quickly, but evaluating its quality, maintainability, and correctness remains essential. Understanding decorators and the design principles behind them helps developers make better architectural decisions and work more effectively with AI-generated code.

Whether you are already familiar with Python decorators or want to better understand their capabilities, these slides offer practical examples, implementation techniques, and design principles to help you write cleaner, more maintainable Python code.
